judge_assessment.explanation: I confirmed every value the judge cites and then some: the table limit 6; (x^2-16)/(x-4) -> 8; the graph-A limit 4; sum(2n-1, n = 1..5) = 25; the two table entries (sqrt(1.01)-1)/0.01 = 0.4988 and (sqrt(0.99)-1)/(-0.01) = 0.5013 with exact limit 1/2; (x^3-8)/(x^2-4) -> 12/4 = 3; the one-sided graph values 2 and 3; 3/(1 - 1/2) = 6; the conjugate limit 1/6; 203/99 = 2.0505 and 2003/999 = 2.005 with end behaviour 2; the asymptote 3; and the synthesis 31/32 and 1. All correct. This case is also the shard's best answer to the dominant systemic finding, and that belongs on the record rather than being restated as a defect: problems 5, 10 and 12 carry MULTIPLE verify entries under one id so each printed table cell and each requested value is separately checked, and the Quick Answers bank consequently prints "5. 0.4988, 0.5013, 1/2", "10. 2.0505, 2.005, 2" and "12. 31/32, 1" -- exactly what verify-every-printed-answer-slot asks for. Problems 7 and 12 go further and pair their machine entries with a `manual` entry carrying an acceptance standard. Where I part company with a clean 32/32 is the inconsistency this exposes: problems 1 and 3 print the identically shaped demand -- "Say in one sentence why 'undefined at x = 3' does not stop the limit from existing" and "say in one sentence why the open circle does not change the answer" -- and neither has a manual companion, even though the answer key writes out an "Expected sentence" for problem 1. The same sheet declares the pattern on two items and omits it on two others.

strengths_to_preserve: Multi-entry ids: problem 5 verifies both computed table entries AND the exact limit; problem 10 verifies both end-behaviour table entries AND the limit; problem 12 verifies the fifth partial sum, the infinite sum, and carries a manual entry for the explanation. This is the shape the rest of the shard should copy, and it flows through to the Quick Answers bank unchanged.

The two manual entries are written as grading rubrics, not placeholders: problem 7's says to accept any answer comparing the two one-sided values and explicitly "do not accept 'because there is a break in the graph' with no reference to the two one-sided values"; problem 12's says to accept any answer naming the sum as a limit and "do not accept 'you add up all the terms'".

The three graphs are printed once, together, each named (A: g with its hole; B: the piecewise h with solid dot and open circle; C: p with its asymptote dashed), with the directions stating that every problem needing one says which graph it means and that no graph belongs to any other problem. That removes the commonest ambiguity in a graph-reading sheet.

Eight declared traps cover misconceptions specific to limits -- reading 0/0 as the answer, stopping a partial sum one term early, reporting sqrt(1)+1 instead of its reciprocal after rationalizing, using a = 3/2 or a = 1 in a/(1-r), inverting the leading-coefficient ratio, and reading a y-intercept where end behaviour was asked.

root_causes.description: Because the manual companion entry is a convention rather than an enforced rule, the same sheet can apply it correctly to two items and omit it on two others whose printed demand is identical in shape.
evidence: worksheet problem 1: "Say in one sentence why 'undefined at x = 3' does not stop the limit from existing"; verify.json id 1 is one `limit` entry with no manual companion
worksheet problem 3: "say in one sentence why the open circle does not change the answer"; verify.json id 3 is one `limit` entry
the answer key's problem 1 prints an "Expected sentence", so the key already treats it as a graded response
by contrast verify.json ids 7 and 12 each carry a manual entry alongside their machine entries

improvements.title: Problems 1 and 3 require a written sentence with no manual entry, while 7 and 12 in the same sheet declare one
improvements.proposed_change: Add a build gate tests/check_open_response_flags.py, wired into scripts/build.sh next to check_layout.py, that reads the ws_ .tex and the verify JSON together. For each problem body it matches explanation cues (explain / justify / name the error / name the first wrong line / say in one sentence / say what / describe / sketch / state what it tells you / why) and fails the build when that problem id carries no entry of type `manual`. Tighten SKILL.md's rule from "Use manual for ... any explanation/reasoning answer" to the explicit statement that a problem mixing a computed answer with a written justification needs BOTH entries under the same id -- the multi-entry-per-id shape verify.py already supports and that curr-445 already uses correctly.
improvements.regression_test: tests/test_open_response_flags.py::test_explanation_without_manual_entry_fails -- a fixture worksheet whose problem 2 reads "Solve ... then explain in one sentence why the negative candidate is extraneous" with verify.json holding only {"id": 2, "type": "solve", ...} must exit non-zero and name problem 2; the same fixture with an added {"id": 2, "type": "manual"} entry must exit 0. Today no such gate exists, so the first fixture builds green.
improvements.expected_impact: Every written justification the sheet demands becomes visible as a manual-review item (exit 2) instead of being absorbed into a "fully machine-verified" claim, which is what the task prompt asks for.
improvements.risk: Cue matching over prose will over-fire on stems that merely say "show your work"; keep the cue list narrow, exempt ids already typed `manual`, and fixture-lock both the firing and the non-firing case.

case_summary: The strongest verification design in my shard. Twelve interleaved problems connect table, graph, algebra and partial-sum views of a limit; all values are correct; three problems use multiple verify entries under one id so every printed table cell and every requested value is separately checked; and two problems pair machine entries with genuine manual rubrics that say what to reject as well as what to accept. The ACCEPT is right and the judge's manual reviews of problems 7 and 12 are accurate. The one defect is an internal inconsistency the judge did not surface: problems 1 and 3 print the same "say in one sentence why" demand that problems 7 and 12 declare as manual, and they do not declare it -- evidence that the correct pattern is known to the generator but enforced nowhere.
